reviews.context: Two frames extracted from a down-the-line swing video shared in chat after today's lesson with Adrian — one at the top of the backswing, one just after the start of the downswing — compared side by side to check the sequencing the lesson flagged. (A single frame can't show sequencing; this review is only possible because two transition-bracketing frames were available.)

observations.note: Comparing the two frames: the arms and shoulders have already moved down and out toward the ball by the second frame, while the hips have barely started clearing toward the target — consistent with the lesson's diagnosis of the downswing being initiated by the upper body rather than the lower body.

reviews.verdict: This confirms what came up in today's lesson: the downswing is being started by the arms/shoulders instead of the lower body, which pushes the club out and over the ideal path and shows up as the over-the-top move. The fix isn't a separate swing-plane correction — it's getting the hips to initiate the downswing first so the arms are just along for the ride, matching the coach's "let the arms drop" cue.

reviews.context: Toptracer screenshot from the warm-up block of today's session (s-2026-09-27), 50-degree wedge. One shot's numbers shown; user separately reported 8 good strikes and 2 mishits (one toe, one top) across the 10-shot warm-up.

observations.note: 13-degree launch and a 25ft apex are both low for a full 50-degree wedge swing carrying 85 yards — that combination (flat, penetrating flight rather than the higher, softer-landing shot a 50-degree loft normally produces) is the classic signature of a thin or topped strike, not a flush one. It's plausible this particular shot is the 'top' the user mentioned rather than one of the 8 good ones, despite the distance looking reasonable.
First wedge numbers logged (previous stats history was 7-iron only): 89.5mph ball speed, 85.4yd carry, 117yd total. No baseline exists yet for this club to compare against.

reviews.verdict: Distance looks fine on paper, but the launch angle/apex combination doesn't match what a clean 50-degree wedge strike should look like — worth treating this as likely one of today's mishits rather than a good strike, and a reminder that flight shape (not just carry distance) is the tell for contact quality on partial/full wedge shots. Keep using the impact tape from today's plan to confirm toe vs. center vs thin directly rather than inferring it from ball flight.

reviews.context: Toptracer screenshot from the sequencing drill block (25 balls, 7i, step-change-of-direction + pump-drill) of today's session s-2026-09-27. Table showed the 3 most recent shots plus a rolling average; user confirmed the average is the representative number for the full 25-ball block, not the 3 individual shots (which were just whatever happened to be last on screen, including one outlier).

observations.note: Block average (99yd carry, 106mph ball speed, 8-degree launch, 139yd total) is below the ~150yd/131mph baseline but not dramatically — a much steadier picture than the 3 individually-logged shots suggested on their own, once the 53.7yd-offline outlier isn't over-weighted. Consistent with isolating a new sequencing move rather than swinging normally.

Average offline was 6ft (~2yd), direction not shown — much tighter than the individual outlier implied. The 3 logged shots remain real data points, just not representative of the block on their own; the average is the number to trust for this block.

reviews.verdict: Correcting the earlier read: the block average tells a calmer story than the 3 individual shots did — carry and ball speed are down from baseline as expected while grooving a new movement, but not the wild, outlier-driven picture the last 3 shots alone suggested. Numbers alone still can't confirm the sequencing itself has changed (that needs video), so this stays feel-building, not a verdict on progress — but there's no cause for concern here.

reviews.context: Toptracer screenshot from the contact drill block (25 balls, impact tape + coin-under-ball) of today's session s-2026-09-27. User switched from 7i to 8i partway through purely to keep the two blocks visually separate on Toptracer's chart, not for a coaching reason. Table showed the 3 most recent shots plus the block's rolling average; treating the average as the representative number this time, per the correction on the previous block.

observations.note: Block average: 106mph ball speed (identical to the earlier 7i sequencing-block average), but 117yd carry vs that block's 99yd, 12-degree launch vs 8, and 38ft apex vs 21 -- all up despite 8i carrying less loft than 7i. That combination (same speed, better launch conditions) points at cleaner contact, not just a different club.

User's own read -- 'little consistency at the start but felt like finding a good groove in the sequencing toward the end' -- lines up with the numbers: a session that starts rough and trends toward cleaner contact/launch is exactly what better sequencing arriving mid-block would look like.

First 8i numbers logged. The 3 individually-shown shots all missed left (13-36yd), but the block average's offline (38ft, direction not shown) suggests the full 25 shots were more centered than that sample implies -- consistent with the lesson from the prior block not to over-read a handful of shown shots.

reviews.verdict: This reads as real progress within the session, not just noise: contact quality (launch angle, apex) improved from the sequencing block to this one at the same ball speed, matching the user's own sense that the sequencing feel clicked partway through. Left miss shows up in the 3 sampled shots but shouldn't be overweighted given the average tells a steadier story. Worth asking next lesson whether this improved feel held up under the transfer/pressure-test blocks that follow, or was specific to slow, deliberate drill reps.

reviews.context: Toptracer screenshot from the transfer block (20 balls, driver, normal full tee shots) of today's session s-2026-09-27. First driver numbers ever logged. User's own read: 'decently consistent but all a bit short and curving heavy right.'

observations.note: A big, consistent right curve across all 4 rows (108-149ft of curve, 27-77yd final offline right, all in the same direction) on the club with the most club speed and longest swing arc is the textbook place for an over-the-top move to show up hardest -- an outside-in path with the face left open relative to it produces exactly this shape. This is a more direct, current-full-speed signal on the actual fault than the earlier iron drill blocks could give.

Ball speed was genuinely high (143-155mph, average 150) -- matches the 'fast, powerful swing ahead of its consistency' baseline -- but carry (avg 177yd) badly underperforms that speed. Heavy slice spin from the same path issue is almost certainly what's eating the distance, not a lack of power. First driver baseline established.

reviews.verdict: This is the clearest single piece of evidence today: two blocks of sequencing/contact drill work on irons didn't erase the pattern once the driver and full speed came back into it -- the ball flight (big, one-directional right curve) matches the over-the-top diagnosis directly, and it's very likely the same root cause as the toe/top misses at Ramsdale and the short/right pattern here: an outside-in downswing path. Worth naming this specifically to Adrian next lesson as evidence the drills are helping the feel in isolation but haven't yet transferred to full-speed driver swings.

reviews.context: Toptracer screenshot from the pressure test block (15 balls, driver, target/scoring) of today's session s-2026-09-27, the final block. User reported feeling like they'd found 'the right driver feel' but described it as feeling more vertical than their iron swing, and noted they've never had a lesson specifically on driver technique. One of the three visible shots (332yd carry, 117.3yd offline) looks like a likely mis-tracked/anomalous reading rather than a real swing -- logged as shown but not weighted in this interpretation.

observations.note: Block average (193yd carry, 154mph ball speed) is actually this session's best driver distance, ahead of the transfer block's 177yd/150mph -- so whatever changed didn't hurt distance. But miss direction went from one-way right in the transfer block to mixed (two shots pulled left, one huge right outlier) -- less consistent, not more.

The user's description of the new feel as 'more vertical' than irons is worth flagging rather than endorsing: a normal driver swing is generally shallower/flatter than an iron swing (the ball is teed forward and higher, wanting a slightly ascending strike), not steeper. Feeling MORE vertical with driver is a common thing golfers do when they swing harder at it, and a steep, vertical downswing plane is also literally what the over-the-top fault looks like -- so this could be the same sequencing issue showing up more with a longer club and more effort, rather than a genuinely new/correct feel. Numbers and a self-description can't confirm swing plane either way; this needs video or, better, direct coaching, since driver hasn't been covered in a lesson yet.

reviews.verdict: Don't take 'felt like the right driver feel' at face value yet -- the description of it (more vertical) points the opposite direction from what a driver swing normally wants, and overlaps suspiciously with the known over-the-top pattern rather than a fix for it. The result (best distance of the day, but less consistent miss direction than the transfer block) doesn't clearly confirm or deny it either. This is a genuinely good, specific question for Adrian: driver-specific technique has never been covered, and 'should my driver swing feel different from my irons, and how' is worth asking directly rather than guessing from feel alone.

reviews.context: Real video (not stills), driver, filmed from behind/side-on during extra balls hit after the planned session. Extracted at native frame rate (~51-62fps) around the top-of-backswing/transition, giving many frames bracketing that moment -- full sequencing assessment is in scope, not just position checks.

observations.note: Top-of-backswing position itself looks solid: full shoulder turn, good width, hands reach a proper height. The backswing isn't the issue.

Comparing the frame at the top (hips still square, fully coiled) to the very next frames (~0.06-0.08s later): the club and arms have already dropped substantially -- the shaft swings from vertical-behind-the-head down through roughly 45 degrees -- while the hips show almost no rotation yet. The lower body only starts visibly opening a couple of frames after that. This is the arms/club initiating the downswing before the lower body, the same pattern the 9/12 lesson's video review found with the 7-iron (r-2026-09-12-a) -- now confirmed on driver, at full speed, not just irons or drills.

reviews.verdict: This directly answers the open question from the pressure test block: the 'more vertical' feel wasn't a correction, it was the same over-the-top pattern -- arms and club dropping steeply from the top before the hips clear, which is exactly what produces a steep, vertical-feeling downswing and the big right curve seen in both driver blocks today. The backswing and top position are genuinely fine; the fix is still entirely about the transition, matching the coach's existing 'let the arms drop' cue and the step-change/pump-drill work. Worth showing this exact video to Adrian -- it's the clearest evidence yet that the fault is identical on driver and irons, just more visible/costly on the longer club.

reviews.context: Longer real video (~9s), driver, same behind/side-on angle, filmed right after being given a specific in-the-moment cue (start the downswing with a lead-hip turn before the arms move, at ~80% speed). Contains 5 separate full swings back to back. Extracted native-rate frame bursts around the top-of-backswing/transition for 3 of the 5 swings (clear transition frames were captured for swings 1, 2, and 3; swings 4 and 5 were still paused at the top in the sampled frames, so sequencing wasn't assessable for those two from this video).

observations.note: All 3 assessable swings show the same pattern as r-2026-09-27-f: comparing the frame at the top (hips square) to frames ~0.1-0.15s later, the club/arms have already dropped roughly 45 degrees while the hips are still barely rotated. Hip rotation becomes visible only after the arms have started moving, in all 3 cases. The cue given between blocks (hip-first, 80% speed) does not appear to have changed the sequencing in these reps, despite being applied right before filming.

reviews.verdict: Straightforward but not the answer hoped for: the arms-first pattern held across all 3 swings this video could assess, immediately after being given a specific cue to fix it. That's normal, not a bad sign on its own -- a verbal cue rarely overrides a well-grooved pattern in a handful of reps, especially at driver speed -- but it does mean the fix isn't going to come from a single range session of self-directed cueing. The two most useful next steps: (1) go back to slow, isolated pump-drill/step-change reps specifically with the driver (today's drill work was all 7-iron) before trying full-speed transfer again, and (2) bring this video to Adrian rather than continuing to self-diagnose -- a coach watching live can catch the exact moment and give real-time feedback in a way video review after the fact can't.

reviews.context: Old video (~14s, 2 driver swings) from the user's first-ever driving range session, roughly a year before today, shared to check whether sequencing has actually improved since then. Shot from a different angle than today's footage -- face-on/target-side, not behind/side-on -- which limits how directly the transition can be compared: this angle makes hip-vs-arm rotation timing genuinely harder to isolate than today's angle, since the whole upper body rotates toward the camera together rather than showing a clean side profile of the hip line versus the arms.

observations.note: In the first swing, a small knee-flex/weight-shift is visible in the couple of frames just before the club visibly starts dropping from the top -- consistent with (not conclusive proof of) an earlier lower-body initiation than today's swings showed, where the club had already dropped ~45 degrees before any lower-body movement was visible. In the second swing, the drop happened within about 2 sampled frames (~0.03s), too fast at this angle to confidently resolve which moved first. Given the angle limitation, this is a real observation worth naming, not a confirmed diagnosis either way.

One clearly comparable thing regardless of angle: the pause at the top lasted noticeably longer in this old video (many more static frames before any downswing motion) than in any of today's driver swings, where the drop started within a few frames of reaching the top. Tempo/transition speed has picked up over the year, whatever's true about the sequencing itself.

reviews.verdict: Can't give a clean yes/no on whether the specific sequencing fault has improved since this video -- the camera angle is too different from today's to make a confident before/after call, and that's a real limitation, not a way of avoiding the question. What's genuinely visible either way: tempo has changed (a much shorter pause at the top now), and there's a hint of earlier leg/weight movement in the older footage that today's swings didn't show, though it's not conclusive from this angle. The practical fix for 'am I improving' going forward is boring but real: film future range sessions from the same angle (behind/side-on, like today) so a real year-from-now comparison is actually possible, rather than relying on old footage shot for a different purpose.

reviews.context: Old iron swing (~1 year old, per user), this time filmed from behind/side-on -- the same angle as today's footage, unlike the earlier face-on driver clip (r-2026-09-27-h). This is the first genuinely direct, apples-to-apples comparison to today's swings.

observations.note: Same pattern as every swing checked today: at the top, hips square. Within about 4 frames (~0.07s), the club has already dropped 30-45 degrees while the hips are still barely rotated; hip rotation only becomes clearly visible a few frames later, closer to impact. From a directly comparable angle, this looks the same as today's driver swings (r-2026-09-27-f, r-2026-09-27-g) -- not visibly better or worse.

reviews.verdict: This is the direct comparison the earlier face-on video couldn't give: from the same angle, a year apart, the transition looks the same -- arms/club initiating before the hips clear, both then and now. That's a genuinely honest answer to 'am I not getting any better': on this specific fault, from this evidence, no clear change is visible over a year. That's worth taking seriously rather than softening, but it also points at what's actually needed -- this fault has been present long enough and through enough unsupervised practice that it's very unlikely to resolve through more range time alone. It needs sustained, coached repetition (ideally checked in most lessons going forward, not just when it comes up), not another solo session.
